claims.text: Compositional differences between equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary or ternary subsets cause measurable differences in stacking-fault energy.
Differences in stacking-fault energy alter the relative activation of deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
Changes in twinning and dislocation-slip activity produce differences in strain hardening.
Changes in twinning and dislocation-slip activity produce differences in ductility.
Changes in twinning and dislocation-slip activity alter failure behavior.
The compared alloys can be prepared as single-phase FCC materials with similar grain sizes and textures.
Lower stacking-fault energy favors nucleation of deformation twins.
Deformation twins act as secondary carriers of strain.
Deformation twinning alters the progression to failure.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors continuous dislocation slip.
A subset with lower effective stacking-fault energy than the quinary baseline will exhibit greater twin density.
A subset with lower effective stacking-fault energy than the quinary baseline will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate at low-to-moderate strains.
A subset with lower effective stacking-fault energy may exhibit earlier localized deformation and failure than the quinary baseline.
A subset with higher stacking-fault energy than the quinary baseline will exhibit reduced deformation twinning.
A subset with higher stacking-fault energy than the quinary baseline will exhibit a more uniform dislocation-slip response.
The proposed mechanism applies under matched single-phase FCC microstructures, room temperature, and constant strain rate.
